description: Our team consists of students who are interested in software, coding, and space, and who are passionate about learning new things. We love coding, exploring technology, and conducting research on space. We want to develop ourselves to generate new ideas, find solutions to the problems we encounter, and work together on great projects. Our goal is to produce successful work as a team while both learning and having fun.
summary: Our project is a remotely controlled Mars robot developed to provide open-source data support for the process of mapping rocks on the surface of Mars. It was designed using an Arduino, a motor driver, six DC motors, an HC-06 Bluetooth module, 12V Li-ion batteries, and a pressure-temperature sensor. By comparing the environmental data we collect with our robot against computer-generated models, we analyze the effects of temperature and pressure on the rocks. In this project, we do not generate a map directly; instead, we aim to provide space researchers and the scientific community with a secure, raw, and processable data infrastructure so they can create their own maps. This approach lays a crucial foundation that will guide future exploration and mapping efforts in Mars’ harsh conditions. Developed in line with the open-source philosophy, this system aims to contribute to the scientific community by fostering collaboration among young people and researchers interested in space technology.
details:
1. Why do we want to go to Mars? And why did we design a vehicle for this purpose?

We want to investigate whether conditions suitable for life ever existed on Mars and to better understand the planet. For this reason, we designed a six-wheeled exploration robot capable of navigating challenging terrain and collecting environmental data to study Mars’ surface and atmosphere.

2. What challenges on Mars does the vehicle we designed address? How is it different from other vehicles?

Mars features rocky and rugged terrain, a dusty environment, and low temperatures. These conditions pose significant challenges for exploration vehicles. Our robot’s six-wheeled design was developed to help it navigate uneven surfaces. Our robot is controlled by an Arduino Uno, a motor driver board, and a Bluetooth module. Our project integrates the mobility system with environmental sensing capabilities. The most significant difference is that it combines these two features in a single robot.

3. What data and information do we want to collect from Mars?

We want to gather information about Mars’ atmospheric pressure and temperature conditions. We aim to take pressure and temperature measurements using the MS5611 sensor on our robot. These measurements will help us examine atmospheric conditions and evaluate the data we collect.

4. Where and how will we use the data we collect from Mars?

We will use the data we collect to study Mars’ environmental conditions and compare measurement results. This information can help us better understand the Martian atmosphere and contribute to the development of future exploration vehicles.
dataRefs: The general increase in pressure on Mars between the 31st and 93rd days is an indication that the mass of the Martian atmosphere increases as the southern hemisphere enters spring. This occurs because the south pole receives progressively more sunlight and carbon dioxide evaporates from the south polar ice cap during winter. As a result of this effect, the atmosphere expands and contracts by approximately 30% each year. The curves also show a strong daily pressure variation of about 10 percent on Mars, peaking around 7 a.m. and reaching a minimum around 4 p.m. This daily pressure cycle stems from the “thermal tide”—a global-scale pressure wave in the Martian atmosphere caused by sunlight heating the surface and the atmosphere.
